plain: An open standard for running programs (called kernels) on GPUs, CPUs and other processors, from many different makers.
The industry group (a non-profit consortium) that writes and publishes OpenCL and other standards such as Vulkan and SPIR-V.
The official text that defines OpenCL. It comes in parts: the API spec, the OpenCL C spec, and the SPIR-V environment spec.
The set of C functions and constants a program calls to use OpenCL, such as clCreateBuffer.
where: API spec, chapters on the platform layer and runtime.

plain: The language the small programs that run on the device (kernels) are written in. It has its own versions, such as 1.2 and 3.0.
A function written in OpenCL C that runs on the device, usually many copies at once.
One vendor's OpenCL implementation installed on a machine. A platform exposes one or more devices.
A processor OpenCL can run kernels on, such as a GPU.
The software from a hardware maker that implements OpenCL for its devices.
A machine-readable file (xml/cl.xml) listing every OpenCL function, constant, type and extension, with their versions and dependencies. Tools generate parts of the C headers from it.
The C files a program includes (for example CL/cl.h) that declare the OpenCL functions and constants.
An optional add-on to OpenCL with its own name, such as cl_khr_semaphore. A device reports which extensions it supports; a program checks before using one.
Name prefixes that show who defined an extension: KHR means approved by the Khronos working group, EXT means a multi-vendor extension, and a company name means a single vendor's.
What a device claiming a given OpenCL version must provide, apart from the features that version makes optional. The opposite of an extension.
An extension whose features were moved into core in a later version. The extension name still exists and devices keep reporting it, but programs can now rely on the core version.
A registry label meaning the Khronos working group formally approved the extension as final.
An extension marked as still changing. The spec says its features may be added, removed, or changed in non-backward compatible ways.
Used here for an extension that has no ratified label in the registry. That includes all vendor extensions and some drafts.
where: This tool's definition, from the registry.

plain: Still present but discouraged. The spec says functionality is never removed in minor versions, so deprecated items stay in the headers.
Since OpenCL 3.0, many features that earlier versions required (shared virtual memory, pipes, device-side enqueue and others) are optional. A device says whether it supports each one.
The part of the API spec that lists each optional feature, how to detect it, and what each function does when the feature is absent.
A name such as __opencl_c_subgroups that the OpenCL C compiler defines when it supports an optional language feature.
A question a program asks about a device or platform, such as clGetDeviceInfo with a constant naming what to ask.
A setting a programmer defines before including the headers to choose which OpenCL version's functions are visible, such as 300 for 3.0.
A preprocessor condition in a header (such as #ifdef CL_VERSION_3_1) that makes declarations visible only when the chosen target version is high enough.
The system that lets several vendors' OpenCL drivers live on one machine. A small loader library forwards each call to the right driver.
The list of function pointers (cl_icd_dispatch) the ICD loader uses to forward calls. Its order is fixed, so new functions are added at the end.
Application binary interface: the exact memory layout and call conventions that compiled programs and drivers rely on. Changing it can break software that was built earlier.
A compact binary format for kernels, an alternative to shipping OpenCL C source. IL means intermediate language.
A group of kernel copies (work-items) that can synchronise and share fast local memory.
A smaller set of work-items inside a work-group that run closely together and can exchange data directly.
Shared virtual memory: memory the host program and the device can both access through the same pointers. Optional since OpenCL 3.0.
An OpenCL C feature that lets one pointer type refer to memory in several address spaces. Optional since 3.0; device-side enqueue and pipes depend on it.
Letting a kernel on the device start other kernels without going back to the host. Optional since 3.0.
A first-in first-out memory object kernels use to pass data to each other. Optional since 3.0.
A recorded list of commands that can be submitted many times, like a saved graph of work. Defined by the extension cl_khr_command_buffer.
A synchronisation object that can order work between queues, or between OpenCL and other APIs. Defined by cl_khr_semaphore.
FULL_PROFILE is the complete feature set; EMBEDDED_PROFILE lets small devices omit some requirements.
The Khronos test suite an implementation must pass before it may call itself conformant. This tool does not run it and cannot say what a change would cost it.
A named, fixed point in the specification's history, such as v3.1.2.
The spec's self-contained page for one function or constant.
A hypothetical version of the headers this tool generates to test an idea. It is not a Khronos file.
Read directly from a Khronos source file by a script. It cannot drift; rerun the script and it is true again or the script fails.
Computed by a stated rule from extracted data. Check the rule if you doubt the result.
A keyword or pattern guess. A pointer for reading, not a verdict. Counts can be too high or too low.
A fact read from one real device on the author's machine. One device is not representative.
Something the public sources cannot tell you, such as test cost, which devices ship what, or working-group intent.
